title: How Search Results Get Confirmed as Memory

beats.h: How Search Results Get Confirmed as Memory
paras: Search is the entrance to a memory system. But a search result isn't memory by itself.
A single question can surface several candidates.
The problem isn't finding a lot of candidates. It's deciding which one should actually be interpreted.
diagrams:
Question
   ↓
Search
   ↓
Candidate A
Candidate B
Candidate C

paras: Search candidates don't all come from one database.
A text search result can be a candidate. A vector search result can be a candidate. A graph Node can be found directly. Other stored objects like Records or Decisions can connect to a question too.
What matters is that these candidates aren't all the same shape. A search result can be a document Chunk. A graph result can be a Concept. A Record is a distinct kind of recorded object.
Chapter 7 already showed that this system doesn't pick when things are ambiguous. The question here is how that principle actually gets enforced.

If two candidates look equally plausible, the point isn't that some rule has to justify picking one of them: the absence of any basis for picking is itself a valid outcome. Picking the wrong Node drags everything explored afterward in the wrong direction, which is exactly why not picking counts as a normal response from the system, not a failure.

Understanding resolution as a simple similarity threshold misses this structure. Search is the stage that produces candidates. Resolution is the stage that checks whether one of them can actually be identified.
This split lets a search system stay broad while retrieval, and stay conservative at the resolution step.
beats.h: Candidate and Resolution Are Different States
diagrams:
Search = what could be relevant?
Resolution = which of these is it pointing at?

paras: Once one Node is resolved, the system can start assembling material around it.

The graph matters here. If a search result lands on a particular Concept, the Records and relationships connected to that Concept can be explored. Chunks from related documents can also serve as evidence.
A search result stops being just a list of text and becomes the starting point for further navigation.
beats.h: Material Gets Pulled From the Resolved Node
diagrams:
resolved Node
      ↓
related Concepts
related Records
related Decisions
      ↓
documents / excerpts
      ↓
answer material

paras: A Concept is a unit of meaning the system works with. A Record is an object that preserves a specific fact or observation.

A search result landing on a Concept doesn't mean its attached records should automatically be treated as identical to it. Nor does a Record being found make it the same as the concept it describes. After resolution, these different objects still have to be read as connected but distinct.
beats.h: A Record Is a Different Kind of Object Than a Concept

paras: An Episode records something that happened, in chronological order. So an Episode isn't a resolution target in the same way a Concept or Record is. An Episode is material for recalling what happened, and when, along a timeline.
Search decides what to look for. Episodes add the temporal context around it.
diagrams:
Question
   ↓
relevant Node
   ↓
related Episode
   ↓
temporal context

paras: The same concept can be expressed in different languages. A Korean question can point at a Concept or Record written in English. Plain string matching isn't enough here.

Embedding helps close this gap in semantic space across languages. But final resolution shouldn't rely on vector similarity alone. So language differences get handled by broadening candidates at the search stage, and confirming identity through structure at the resolution stage.
beats.h: Language Differences Are Also a Post-Search Problem

paras: Sometimes there's no result. Sometimes there aren't enough candidates. Sometimes the candidates can't be told apart.
In these cases, the system doesn't force a memory into existence.

This isn't a failed search: it's an important system state. One of the most dangerous outcomes in a memory system is resolving a target with no basis for it, and letting every downstream step treat that target as fact.
beats.h: Search Failure Is Also a Valid State
diagrams:
no candidate → no resolution
ambiguous candidates → no resolution
beats.claim: So VINC's retrieval structure needs both the ability to find, and the ability not to choose.
